summary: M.I.Y.H. (Mars In Your Hands) turns NASA orbital and rover data into a hyperlocal EVA planner for the first humans on Mars. After a cinematic landing in Gale crater, users plan a walk over the real terrain Curiosity drove: an A* engine traces the safest route, explains every blocked spot and checks whether the oxygen is enough to come back. The planned route can also be explored in a 3D Unity view built on Gale’s real elevation data. Then they walk it: simulated suit and body telemetry feeds transparent health rules (GO, caution, abort), narrated by an assistant. Every layer is labeled REAL, DERIVED, MODELLED or SIMULATED, so anyone can see what is NASA data and what is a model. Today’s maps show Mars from orbit; M.I.Y.H. answers the astronaut’s question at walking scale: can we go there, and come back safely?
details:
REPOSITORY

What it does. M.I.Y.H. is a six-chapter journey: (1) a landing in Gale crater with real Curiosity entry data, (2) MarsWalk, a mission planner, (3) a live walk simulation, (4) a 3D terrain view in Unity using real elevation data of Gale crater, (5) the technical references, and (6) the project story. The idea behind it: human footprints over 60 years of robot tracks.

How it works. Three layers, each one checkable:

  • Real data. NASA Mars Trek tiles, the MOLA elevation model, Curiosity's REMS weather, its traverse and 62 boxwork waypoints, DONKI solar particle events and the Access Mars terrain mesh of Gale.
  • Deterministic rules. An A* planner finds the lowest-risk route that never crosses forbidden slopes. A health engine applies rules taken from NASA-STD-3001 and Apollo EVA data. The rules decide; the assistant only explains.
  • Interfaces built for a crew. Big type, one main action per screen, states shown with color and shape, and every number next to its limit. It works with the keyboard, respects "reduce motion", uses a typeface designed for low vision and runs in English and Spanish.

What makes it different.

  • Walking scale. Mars Trek and USGS map whole regions; M.I.Y.H. plans the next few hundred meters of an astronaut's walk.
  • Body plus terrain. Slope, oxygen, CO₂, heart rate and radiation are judged together in one GO/NO-GO.
  • Explainable. When a route is blocked, it says why and offers a safe alternative.
  • Honest data. Real, derived, modelled and simulated values are labeled everywhere.
  • Made for outreach. We built it to share Mars, not just to analyze it. A cinematic landing, game-like consoles and hands-on route planning turn real NASA data into an experience anyone can explore and enjoy, from students to the general public.

Validation. We tested the HUELLA rule set with six simulated walks built from NASA physiology data: a normal walk, a fan failure, a suit leak, heat stress, an arrhythmia and a loss of communication. The normal walk raises no alerts, a short scare does not trigger an alarm, and each failure escalates to the expected level. We also recorded telemetry from NASA's SUITS Telemetry Stream Server and converted it to our format.

Who benefits. Mission planners get a walking-scale GO/NO-GO before an EVA. Crews get a console they can read through a helmet visor. Students and teachers explore Mars with real NASA data, always labeled. It runs in any web browser, with nothing to install.

Scalability. Any site with a NASA elevation model can be added, and suit telemetry follows the NASA SUITS format. The same engine works for the Moon and Artemis.

Tools. Three.js, React, TanStack Start and Python for data preparation.

Use of AI

We used Claude, Gemini and NotebookLM to help write code, structure data-cleaning scripts and organize documentation. Every physical value and threshold comes from the NASA sources we list, and the team reviewed each one before using it. No NASA logos were used.
